name: Saint John of the Cross
bio_en: John of the Cross (1542–1591) was a Spanish Carmelite, mystic, and Doctor of the Church, known for his teaching on the spiritual path of purification and union with God.
bio_en_long: Saint John of the Cross is the spiritual father of our Order. Born in 1542 in Fontiveros (Ávila), he entered the Carmelite Order at the age of 21 after a hard and impoverished childhood and youth. He was ordained a priest in 1567, and a year later, together with a fellow brother in Duruelo, he began to live the Carmelite life according to the vision of Saint Teresa of Jesus. He soon became novice master and spiritual director to sisters, priests, and laypeople. As a victim of the conflicts between the original Order and Teresa’s new foundation, he was held for nine months in a monastic prison. After his escape in August 1578, he once again carried out a rich array of activities as a superior, founder of monasteries, and preacher. Yet it is above all his poems and spiritual writings that brought him immortal fame. Thus he became one of the most experienced and, to this day, most highly esteemed spiritual teachers, offering clear and reliable guidance. He died on 14 December 1591 in Úbeda (Jaén), respected by some, persecuted and slandered by others. He was canonized in 1726, declared a Doctor of the Church in 1926, and in 1952 named patron saint of Spanish poets.

name: Saint Mariam of Jesus Crucified
name_de: Heilige Mirjam von Jesus, dem Gekreuzigten
bio_en: Saint Mariam of Jesus Crucified (1846-1878), the "Little Arab," born in the Holy Land, a humble Carmelite who learned to read and write as an adult, founded Carmelite monasteries in the Holy Land and India. Her simple and radiant life, led by the Holy Spirit, invites us to let ourselves be loved and transformed by Jesus.
bio_en_long:
Mariam Baouardy was born on 5 January 1846 in Ibillin, in Upper Galilee, into a poor, faith led, Eastern Christian family. After her parents lost twelve boys in infancy, Mariam was born to them thanks to a pilgrimage to Bethlehem. Two years later, her brother Boulos was born, but at three years old she lost both her parents and was entrusted to a paternal uncle, who later moved to Alexandria.

From a very young age, she was marked by a profound spiritual sensitivity, perceiving the eeting nature of life and an invitation to give her heart to God. Not yet 13 years old, she refused an arranged marriage, desiring to consecrate herself entirely to Christ. Mistreated by her uncle, she went to see a former servant of her uncle who pressured her to convert to Islam. She refused, proclaiming her Christian faith. The servant slit her throat and abandoned her in a dark alley. Mariam awoke in a cave, cared for by a woman dressed in blue, whom she would later identify as the Virgin Mary. One woman then led her to a church and left her there. Mariam began to work as a servant for families in Alexandria, Jerusalem, Beirut, and then Marseille, where, in 1865, she entered the Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition. Soon, her mystical gifts began to appear: visions, ecstasies, stigmata, and prophecies. After two years of novitiate, Mariam was not permitted to profess vows.

In June 1867, she joined the Carmel of Pau, France, as a lay sister and took the name Sister Mary of Jesus Crucified. Little and unassuming, she devoted herself to manual labor even as she experienced her mystical gifts with humility. In 1870, she departed for India to help found the Carmel of Mangalore, where she accomplished her work with self-denial. She professed her vows at the end of her novitiate on 21 November 1871. However, misunderstandings related to the manifestations of her mystical gifts began to arise around her, casting doubt on the authenticity of what she was experiencing. The resulting tensions finally led to her being sent back to the Carmel of Pau, France, in 1872. She was warmly welcomed there. There she returned to her simple life as a lay sister amid the affection of her sisters.

In 1875, after many obstacles, she founded the Carmel of Bethlehem. The Lord revealed to her both the location and the construction plans. She supervised the construction thanks to her knowledge of Arabic. She also contributed to the acquisition of land for the future Carmel of Nazareth. While carrying water to the construction workers at the Carmel of Bethlehem, she fell and was seriously injured; gangrene led to her death on 26 August 1878. Her life, marked by humility, service, and mystical experiences, makes her a witness to the invisible universe of faith.

name: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux
bio_en: Thérèse of Lisieux (1873–1897), a Carmelite and Doctor of the Church, taught the “Little Way” of trust and love and is one of the most popular saints of modern times.
bio_en_long: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus, also known as Thérèse of Lisieux, was born in 1872 in Alençon, France. At the age of just 15, she entered the Carmelite monastery in Lisieux, where she lived a life of humility and simplicity, filled with the one desire to work for the salvation and good of all people. She died on 30 September 1897. Thérèse was beatified by Pope Pius XI in 1923 and canonized in 1925. In 1927, she was named patron saint of the missions, and in 1997 Pope John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church.

name: Father Jacques of Jesus
bio_en: Father Jacques of Jesus (1900–1945), a Carmelite and French priest, hid Jewish children during the Second World War, was arrested, and died shortly after the liberation of a concentration camp.
bio_en_long:
Little Lucien, born on 29 January 1900 into a poor family whose daily life was marked by hard work, very soon dreamed of becoming “a great parish priest.” The dechristianized regions and children left to fend for themselves awakened and strengthened his passion as an apostle and educator.

A few months before his ordination to the diaconate, he was appointed to Collège Saint-Joseph in Le Havre, where he discovered the Carmel. On 11 July 1925, he was ordained a priest.

After many inner and outward struggles, he left the Diocese of Rouen with the consent of his archbishop and entered the novitiate of the Discalced Carmelites in Lille in September 1932. He received the name Jacques of Jesus.

He founded and directed the small Collège Sainte-Thérèse-de-l’Enfant-Jésus in Avon, where he developed the many educational gifts of his vocation as an educator. He wanted “his” children to grow into complete human beings, aware of their future responsibilities and carrying within themselves the seed of holiness …

His heart as a man and priest was wounded by the cruel acts of the Nazi regime. Deeply shaken, he took the side of those who were suffering and persecuted.

In January 1943, he took in three Jewish children. On 15 January 1944, the Gestapo arrested the three children and Father Jacques. Before he left, he said these words: “Goodbye, children. Carry on without me!”

name: Saint Teresa of the Andes
bio_en: Teresa of the Andes (1900–1920) was a Chilean Carmelite who became known from a young age for her deep love of Christ and her devotion to life in the convent.
bio_en_long: Saint Teresa of Jesus of the Andes was born on 13 July 1900 in Santiago, Chile. At the age of 19, she entered the Carmelite monastery in the city of Los Andes, but died of typhus less than a year later, on 12 April 1920. She is the first saint of Chile and of the Teresian Carmel in Latin America. The poor and ordinary people of her homeland, in particular, have taken her to their hearts. Pope John Paul II beatified her on 3 April 1987 during his visit to Santiago, Chile. Her canonization took place in Rome on 21 March 1993.

name: The Saints of Carmel
bio_en: The saints of Carmel include a great multitude of men and women who attained holiness in the spirit of Mary of Mount Carmel through contemplation, sacrifice, and service to the Church.

name: Saint Teresa of Ávila
bio_en: Teresa of Ávila (1515–1582) was a Spanish mystic, reformer of Carmel, and Doctor of the Church whose spiritual writings and convent reforms profoundly shaped Western spirituality.
bio_en_long:
Born on 28 March 1515 in Ávila, she came on her father’s side from a Jewish family which, through the purchase of a noble title, had become part of the Spanish aristocracy. On 2 November 1535, she entered the Carmelite convent in her hometown. After years of inner turmoil, as well as receiving God’s grace, she founded her first convent on 24 August 1562.

Thanks to the “new life” bestowed upon her, she became a “restless wanderer,” founding convents and, from 1568 onward, with the help of Saint John of the Cross, monasteries for the friars as well. She also wrote spiritual works that continue to offer guidance to this day. She died in Alba de Tormes on 4 October 1582. She was beatified in 1614 and canonized by Pope Gregory XV in 1622. In 1970, she became the first woman in the Church to be proclaimed a Doctor of the Church.

name: Mary of the Incarnation
bio_en: Sister Mary of the Incarnation was a Carmelite whose spirituality focused particularly on the mystery of Christ’s Incarnation and invited people to contemplate God made man.
bio_en_long: Blessed Marie of the Incarnation made a significant contribution to the spread of the Teresian Carmel in France. Born in Paris in 1566, she was married to Pierre Acarie at the age of 16 and belonged to one of the country’s noblest and wealthiest families. Nevertheless, she remained a deeply devout woman and a loving mother of seven children, charitable to the poor and the sick. After her husband’s death, she asked to be admitted to the Carmel in Amiens, where she made her religious profession as a lay sister in 1615. She died in 1618 at the Carmel in Pontoise. She was beatified in 1791.

name: Our Lady of Mount Carmel
name_de: Unsere Liebe Frau vom Berge Karmel
bio_en: Our Lady of Mount Carmel is a Marian title referring to the biblical Mount Carmel. She is venerated as the patroness of the Carmelite Order and is associated with the scapular.
bio_en_long:
The Carmelite Scapular, often referred to as the “Brown Scapular,” is an important sacramental of the Catholic Church. It consists of two small, square pieces of brown fabric connected by bands and worn over the chest and back. It is an outward sign of devotion to the Virgin Mary, trust in her protection, and the commitment to live according to the Gospel.

Mary teaches us:

  • to be open to God’s will and ready to put it into practice;
  • to listen to God’s word in Sacred Scripture and in everyday life, to reflect on it, and to keep it faithfully in our hearts;
  • to pray and seek God at all times, whether or not we feel his presence;
  • to place our trust in God and believe in his love, even when we may not understand his plans at the moment;
  • to be attentive to the concerns and needs of those around us, and thereby become a sign in our own environment that points to Christ.

name: Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein)
bio_en: Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein, 1891–1942) was a philosopher of Jewish heritage who converted to the Catholic faith, became a Carmelite, and died as a martyr in Auschwitz concentration camp.
bio_en_long:
Saint Teresa Benedicta of the Cross (Edith Stein) was born on 12 October 1891 in Breslau, the daughter of Jewish parents. Despite the example of her deeply devout mother, she consciously gave up praying at the age of 13. Nevertheless, she remained constantly in search of the truth. She devoted herself passionately to the study of philosophy, but found the existential answer to the question of true faith in the autobiography of Saint Teresa of Ávila. She was baptized at the age of 31, on 1 January 1922, entered the Carmelite monastery in Cologne in 1933, and died together with her sister Rosa—who was a member of the Carmelite Third Order—and many others as a victim of the Nazi persecution of the Jews, in the gas chambers of Auschwitz on 9 August 1942.

A woman endowed with unique intelligence and rich spiritual gifts, she left behind numerous philosophical and spiritual works. Pope John Paul II beatified her in Cologne on 1 May 1987 and canonized her in Rome on 11 October 1998. In 1999, together with Saint Bridget of Sweden and Saint Catherine of Siena, he declared her a patron saint of Europe.

name: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection
bio_en: Brother Lawrence of the Resurrection (1614–1691) was a French Carmelite lay brother known for his teaching on the constant presence of God in everyday life.
bio_en_long:
Nicolas Herman was born in 1614 in Lorraine, into a deeply Christian family. At the age of 18, he experienced a decisive spiritual moment, which is recounted here. At that time, he chose a military career and served alongside the Duke of Lorraine. But he came perilously close to death, and an injury forced him to leave the army at the age of 21. During the resulting period of convalescence, he decided to dedicate his life to God. He became a hermit, but did not find the peace he longed for.

Nicolas therefore went to Paris, where he became a footman to a royal adviser. At the age of 26, he decided to enter the monastery of the Discalced Carmelites on Rue Vaugirard as a lay brother. He received the name Lawrence of the Resurrection. For 15 years he served as the community’s cook, and later as its cobbler. The first ten years of his religious life—although he had a healthy awareness of his sins—were scarcely remarkable from a spiritual point of view. But he surrendered himself to the Lord and strove to live simply under God’s gaze in all things, at every hour of the day. In this way, he found peace. It was then that this brother’s charism truly began to radiate: he received numerous visitors, including Fénelon. (François Fénelon was the Archbishop of Cambrai.) Thus Brother Lawrence spent his life in a very simple and faithful relationship with the loving God, to whom he returned on 12 February 1691, at the age of 77.

The biography written by one of his friends quickly made him known through his message of practising the presence of God. This work spread widely, even beyond Catholic circles, particularly in the English-speaking world. There, the influence of Brother Lawrence has endured to this day.

name: Saint Joseph
bio_en: Saint Joseph, husband of the Virgin Mary and foster father of Jesus, is venerated as the silent just man and faithful protector of the Church and families.

name: Saint Elisabeth of the Trinity
bio_en: Elisabeth of the Trinity (1880–1906) was a French Carmelite whose spirituality was shaped by the indwelling presence of the Most Holy Trinity in the heart of the baptized person.
bio_en_long: Saint Elizabeth of the Trinity lived to be only 26 years old, five of them in the Carmelite monastery in Dijon, France. Nevertheless, when she died on 9 November 1906, she was convinced that she was “going home to the light, to love, to life.” Through her artistic gifts, she brought much joy to people, but she did not allow herself to become attached to them, for her true home was elsewhere. She was beatified on 25 November 1984 and canonized on 16 October 2016.

name: Saint Elijah
bio_en: The prophet Elijah is regarded as the spiritual father of the Carmelites. His zeal for the one true God and his experience of God at Horeb have shaped the spirituality of the Order.

name: Louis Martin and Zélie Martin (parents of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux)
name_de: Louis Martin und Zélie Martin (Eltern der hl. Thérèse von Lisieux)
bio_en: Louis and Zélie Martin, the parents of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, lived a deeply Christian marriage and were canonized together as role models of holy marriage and family life.
bio_en_long: Saint Louis Martin, born in 1823, was a jeweller; Saint Marie Zélie, born in 1831, made Alençon lace. Their marriage was blessed with nine children, only five of whom survived. The youngest was Saint Thérèse of Lisieux. As exemplary Christian parents, they nurtured in their children a zeal for the missions, love for the poor, and devotion to Mary. After his wife’s death in 1877, Louis moved to Lisieux, where he witnessed his daughters enter religious life and endured severe suffering during the final years of his life. He died in 1894. The couple was beatified in Lisieux on 19 October 2008 and canonized in Rome on 18 October 2015.
